title: Log-space MLE via multistart Levenberg-Marquardt through the forward model attains near-CRB accuracy
text: Because noise is tiny (sigma=1e-3), the Fisher condition number is moderate (~48), and the CRB rel_l2 floor is ~0.019, the likelihood is locally well-conditioned and close to Gaussian in log k. A bounded LM solver working in log-parameter space with a few multistarts should converge to the global MLE for nearly all samples. Its val rel_l2 should then be within about 1.5x of the CRB floor, i.e. below 0.03. The forward operator F: k -> sensor traces is smooth on the box [0.5,2]^4, since an explicit FD solution is a rational/polynomial map of k. The harness-computed Fisher information shows all four parameters are locally identifiable. In this small-noise regime the MLE is asymptotically efficient, so it should approach the CRB. The log transform matters for two reasons: diffusion time scales roughly like 1/k, so log k flattens the curvature, and it enforces positivity. Multistart guards against secondary minima. These can occur because k1 and k4 are only weakly seen through the decayed tails of the pulse, and because the outer segments couple to the inner ones. context.forward exactly matches the data-generating simulator, including the explicit FD scheme, 40 points, 200 steps and the sensor indices Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3, so the least-squares objective is the negative log-likelihood The explicit scheme is stable over the whole box (dt*k_max/dx^2 <= 1/2), so F is smooth with no blow-up The forward-call budget allows about 4 starts x 30 iterations per sample over 750 validation samples within 120s spread across workers

If the error is uniformly above the CRB, the forward model available to us differs from the data generator (model error) or the bounds clip the estimates, and we should check the residual norm against sqrt(n_obs)*sigma.

title: MMSE posterior mean beats the MLE for the weakly identified boundary segments k1, k4 under the box prior
text: rel_l2 is a squared-error loss, so the Bayes-optimal estimator is the posterior mean, not the mode. For k1 and k4 the CRB std is about 2% and the uniform box prior truncates the likelihood near 0.5 and 2.0. A hybrid approach should therefore reduce val rel_l2 by at least 10% relative to the best pure-physics MLE arm, with the gain concentrated in k1 and k4. The hybrid uses a learned torch_mlp initializer, then LM refinement in log space, then an importance-sampled posterior mean on the Laplace approximation. Decision theory says that under squared loss with a known prior the MMSE estimator minimises expected loss, and the MLE is suboptimal wherever the posterior is non-Gaussian or truncated. The boundary segments see the pulse only after it has diffused through the inner segments, which gives a flatter likelihood in k1 and k4. The learned initializer removes the multistart cost and the risk of local minima. A net trained on 3000 simulated pairs gives about 0.05-0.1 error, which is well inside the basin of attraction for Gauss-Newton given cond ~48. The posterior-mean step then corrects for boundary truncation. The prior is exactly i.i.d. uniform on [0.5,2] as stated

data.if_fails: If there is no gain over the MLE, the posterior is effectively Gaussian and untruncated for most samples, so the MLE is already near-Bayes and the remaining error is at the CRB floor, which is irreducible. author: researcher-ml
title: Amortized MLP initializer + few-step Gauss-Newton/LM refinement with MMSE correction (hybrid)
text: A torch_mlp trained on simulated pairs lands inside the basin of the per-sample likelihood. A learned map's error is set by approximation error and finite training data, not by the noise floor. A physics refinement removes most of that approximation error at a cost of a few Jacobian solves per sample. The learned initializer avoids LM multistart cost and local minima. The weakly identified k1 and k4 (edge segments, sensors at indices 5 and 35) have posteriors that can be truncated by the [0.5, 2] box. There the MMSE estimate should beat the mode on squared-error metrics. The MLP initializer has per-parameter error small enough (roughly <10%) to lie in the LM basin of attraction. The harness forward model is the same simulator that generated the data (40-point explicit FD, 200 steps), so there is no model discrepancy. 8 LM iterations on 750 val samples plus training fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit. author: researcher-ml
title: Purely amortized inverse map: MLP on log-k targets with noise-matched augmentation
text: A torch_mlp trained on raw sensor time series has two key features: log-conductivity targets, which match the multiplicative scale of a diffusion coefficient, and on-the-fly Gaussian noise augmentation at the true sigma, which regularizes toward the noisy-data posterior. The map from (k1..k4) to temperatures is smooth but nonlinear: diffusion time scales go roughly as 1/k, so log-k linearizes much of the dependence. With 3000 samples in a 4-D parameter space, a well-regularized MLP should approximate the conditional mean E[k|y]. Under squared loss, that is the Bayes-optimal estimator. This tests whether amortization alone is enough, which matters as the cheap fallback and as the baseline the hybrid must beat. 3000 training samples are enough for an MLP to approximate the posterior mean over a 4-D prior to a few-percent error. The noise_scale parameter is expressed relative to the true noise std (1.0 = sigma). If it is absolute, the augmentation is mis-scaled. Raw features with standard scaling keep the informative early-time and late-time decay information. Log features could blow up on near-zero late-time readings.

title: Learned initializer plus forward-model LM refinement reaches the noise-limited (CRB) regime
text: The remaining error after a kernel-ridge initializer is mainly an optimization or approximation error, not an information limit. Refining each sample with a few bounded Levenberg-Marquardt iterations through the exact forward model, in log-k space, should then bring test rel_l2 down to about 1-1.5x the Cramér–Rao floor (≈0.019-0.028). That is well under the 0.05 target and clearly better than any purely data-driven arm. Several facts point the same way. The simulator is the exact data-generating model: same explicit finite-difference scheme, 40 nodes, 200 steps, same sensor indices. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=0.001. So the Gaussian likelihood is exactly specified, and least squares is the MLE. The diagnostics give a median Fisher condition number of 48 and a CRB rel_l2 floor of 0.0186. The local problem is therefore well posed, and an efficient estimator should land near the floor. The main risk for pure LM is multimodality or slow convergence from the prior centre, because k1 and k4 are weakly determined: the sensors sit inside segments and the Gaussian pulse starts at 0.5, so the outer segments see little flux early on. A learned initializer that already sits in the right basin removes that risk. The log transform respects positivity and evens out curvature across [0.5, 2]. The harness forward model is the same discretization that generated the data, so there is no model-form error. The noise is exactly i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=0.001, so least squares is the MLE. The kernel-ridge initializer lands within the LM basin of attraction for most samples. The CRB computed at 32 prior draws is representative of the whole prior box. The forward-call budget allows about 750 samples x 15 iterations within 120s.

data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid with (a) the kernel-ridge init alone and (b) the CRB floor 0.0186. The hypothesis is refuted on any of three outcomes. First, hybrid val rel_l2 > 0.035 (more than 1.9x CRB). Second, the gain over the init alone is under 20%. Third, the per-parameter errors for k1 and k4 exceed 2x their CRB std, which would indicate convergence failures or model mismatch. The diagnostic is the distribution of normalized residuals per sample: if the MLE is correct, chi^2/dof should be ≈1, and samples far above that show non-convergence.
data.if_fails: Each failure mode points to a different cause. If the error is far above the CRB while chi^2/dof is ≈1, the CRB at 32 draws is unrepresentative, likely near the box edges where clipping or bias dominate; the fix is the posterior_mean estimator. If chi^2/dof >> 1, either convergence failed (fix: more iterations or starts) or the forward model mismatches the data generator, which is a simulation-fidelity issue. If the error barely improves over the init, the init was already at the noise floor.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Control: an amortized neural inverse map trained with noise augmentation falls short of forward-model refinement
text: This is a competing explanation tested as a control. With 3000 training draws, a noise-augmented MLP from raw sensor traces to log k may already approach the CRB, which would make forward-model refinement unnecessary. Our counter-prediction is that it will not. The MLP should reach rel_l2 below 0.05 but stay at least 25% worse than the hybrid arm, because the learning error at n=3000 in 4-D is not negligible next to the 1.9% floor, especially for the weakly determined k1 and k4. The inverse map is smooth, 4-D and well conditioned, so an MLP should learn it well. Noise augmentation (fresh sigma=0.001 draws on each pass) teaches the network the actual measurement distribution instead of memorising 3000 fixed noise realizations. That is a sensor-model-aware regularizer. If this arm matches the hybrid, the 'physics refinement is needed' explanation is falsified, and we save forward-model budget. Running it gives the team a clean ablation that separates the information limit from the estimator limit. The training features are generated with the same noise model as val and test. noise_scale=1.0 adds noise relative to the specified sigma, so the effective noise variance at train time is about the true noise variance, with no mismatch. Standard scaling of raw traces keeps the small-amplitude late-time information that discriminates k1 and k4. 150-300 epochs on 3000 samples fit within the per-experiment limit on CPU.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Minimum-MSE (posterior-mean) refinement beats MLE when the error metric is squared: hybrid learned-init + Laplace/importance-sampled MMSE
text: We usually treat this as a point-estimation (MLE/least-squares) problem, but the metric is a squared relative error averaged over the prior. That makes the Bayes-optimal estimator the posterior mean, not the mode. Hypothesis: a hybrid method beats MAP/MLE refinement from the same initializer by at least 5% relative in val rel_l2, and reaches val rel_l2 <= 0.03. The hybrid is an amortized torch_mlp initializer, followed by bounded LM in log-conductivity space and a posterior-mean estimator from importance sampling on the Laplace approximation under the box prior. The gain should come mostly from the poorly determined end segments k1 and k4, where the posterior is widest and most truncated by the [0.5, 2] box. The diagnostics put the CRB rel_l2 floor near 0.0186. The per-parameter relative std for k1 and k4 (0.022 and 0.018) is 3-4x that of k2 and k3, so the end segments dominate the error. When the posterior is wide and clipped by a box prior, the mode sits on or near the boundary while the mean is pulled inward. MLE then incurs avoidable squared error, exactly the quantity rel_l2 measures. This borrows the Bayesian decision-theory view (choose the estimator that matches the loss) and applies it to PDE parameter identification, where LM/MLE is the default. Working in log space respects positivity and makes the Laplace approximation more Gaussian for a scale-type parameter like conductivity. The learned initializer avoids local minima from multimodal misfits, so we need fewer LM multistarts and stay within compute. The forward model available through context.forward matches the data-generating simulator, so there is no model discrepancy. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 0.001, as stated, so the Gaussian likelihood is correctly specified. The posterior is unimodal near the learned initializer, so a Laplace proposal centred at the LM optimum has adequate importance-sampling efficiency with 128 samples. A log transform makes the local posterior closer to Gaussian than linear space does. rel_l2 is computed on the raw conductivities, averaged over samples.

title: Amortized MMSE without a forward model: a noise-augmented neural regressor on log-temperature features reaches the 0.05 target
text: Using the forward model at inference may be unnecessary here. The prior has only 4 dimensions and there are 3000 training samples, so the inverse map is smooth and low-dimensional and the sample count may suffice. Sensor readings are mostly positive and well above the noise level, so the harness's log feature transform is stable.
